title: Curing patellar tendinitis (part. 2): Rehab & precautions
summary: His training-based method to heal patellar tendinitis, which he had for nearly two years: not rest or painkillers, but a progressive box squat protocol (tall box, empty bar, slow negative, building volume to 135 lbs for 15 reps, then lower boxes, then free squats below parallel with a wider, posterior-chain stance), followed by high-rep 135 'widowmaker' sets to rebuild the quads, then conservative strength rebuilding with elastic knee wraps placed to stabilise the tendon. Avoid impact sports and heavy hip hinges early.

claims.claim: Rest does not heal patellar tendinitis: the tendon was inflamed by a faulty movement pattern (friction) or overwork, and once inflamed it re-flares quickly even after two weeks off, getting progressively worse.
Sending blood to an inflamed tendon makes it feel better and helps it heal.
The three-part fix: correct the movement pattern, manage frequency and tonnage so you don't worsen it, and build the muscles that take strain off the tendon.

He is against painkillers and anti-inflammatories for tendinitis (not medical advice): pain is a signal, and masking it lets you keep wearing down the tendon until it snaps or stays fragile; they always made it worse for him.
He had such severe tendinitis he could barely walk, climb stairs or sleep, and healed it 100%, returning to heavy squatting.
Box squats retrain the squat pattern while working the muscles that support the tendon, without excessive depth that re-aggravates the injury.

Tendinitis gets into your head: anticipating pain at the knee break makes it entrenched, and favoring the other knee risks injuring that one too. Rest 1-2 days to get over the emotional hump, then return to the gym.

Box squat protocol: start with the tallest box that lets you break at the knee, empty bar, very slow negative, touch the box then explode up; e.g. 5x5, add reps, and when you reach 12-15 reps for 5-6 sets add weight.
Add weight only as pain dissipates; the knee break where pain concentrates becomes duller the more you box squat.
Don't load heavy: once you can do 135 lbs (about 15 reps easy) on a box, move to a lower box and restart with an empty bar.
The box squat work effectively replaces leg days while injured, on top of the rest of your training.
Do the rehab every 2-3 days, not daily; squatting every day aggravates tendinitis. Exercise the joint, rest, repeat.
Patellar tendinitis is often caused by dive-bombing the negative and using the tendon's elastic energy to rebound, which is not the right way to squat for muscle or health.
A slow negative lets you track your knees, control shin angle and descend by lengthening the hamstrings and using the glutes; many tendinitis sufferers are quad dominant.
Box squats as an accessory for high-bar squatting are not smart: with a wide stance and the box tight behind the knees they become a hip hinge, not knee flexion (fine only for low bar).
Reducing knee stress moves it elsewhere; ideally to hamstrings and glutes, but overdoing it shifts it to the lower back, which is why you relearn the pattern with low weight.
After 135 on the low box, remove the box, go below parallel with an empty bar and use the chance to relearn your whole squat, since the squat probably caused the injury; he relearned his form 100%.
He used the concept of 'opening the groin' (from Ed Coan via Super Training) to create space to sit into: more posterior chain, knees tracking forward less, shins more vertical.
The more the knees travel forward, the more the quads and the knee joint are taxed; a slightly wider stance with knees opened out spares the knee.
Graduate from the free squat stage only once you can squat below parallel; above-parallel half squats put more shear force on the knee.
Rehabbing tendinitis is never painless; the pain becomes dull. If a session gets too painful, stop and go home.
Once 135 for 15 is easy, do 'widowmakers' with 135: 25-30 reps for 5-6 sets, to flood the tendon area with blood and act as nucleus overload for the quads.
'Train your posterior chain' isn't enough for bad knees: the quads protect the patellar tendon, so they must be strong enough to handle knee flexion and deload the tendon.
High-volume squats regained size on his atrophied quads.
Stay in the widowmaker phase as long as possible: it masters the new technique, rebuilds cardio, and avoids snapping something; never rush an injury.
He had patellar tendinitis for close to two years; the pain persisted from the 135 widowmakers up to roughly 285-295 lbs squats.
After 135 widowmakers he jumped (he thinks) to 185 lbs with lower rep ranges, no more widowmakers.

Knee sleeves give pressure that's too uniform; use short elastic knee wraps (not stiff powerlifting wraps) angled to press on the patellar tendon so it moves and rubs less, letting you load the quads more.
Don't wrap too tight: a tendon with no room to move can tear.
For pain below the kneecap, an X-shaped bandage holds the tendon in place; for pain at the kneecap, wrap around the kneecap. Always wrap from inside to outside to match pushing the knees out.
The rebuilding phase must be as conservative as possible.
His pain went away when his quads reached about 23 inches, because the leg muscles could now protect the tendon; he never scanned it and only cares that he's pain-free and squats heavy.
During rehab avoid impact sports, basketball and running on concrete; keep the knee calm outside training.
Avoid heavy hip hinges in the earliest rehab phases; later add more hamstring work. Hinge pain disappears much earlier than squat pain (conventional deadlift; no data on sumo).
Any hip hinge working hamstrings and glutes helps since they are the antagonists that assist the negative; strong, cautious people rarely get hurt.

exercises.name: Box squat (rehab)
cues: touch the box then explode up
progress to 12-15 reps x 5-6 sets then add weight
cap at 135 lbs then lower the box
exercises.why: retrains the knee break and movement pattern, works the muscles around the tendon, sends blood

exercises.name: Free squat below parallel (rehab)
cues: open the groin, knees out not forward
exercises.why: relearn the squat with more posterior chain and less knee stress

exercises.name: Widowmaker squats
exercises.why: blood flow to tendon, quad nucleus overload, technique mastery, cardio

exercises.name: Elastic knee wraps / bandage
cues: X shape for lower tendon pain
exercises.why: stabilises the tendon so it rubs less while loading the quads

exercises.name: Conventional deadlift / hip hinges
exercises.why: hamstrings/glutes as antagonists support the knee
